lines: Lecture four. Selection, operators and encodings. Who gets to breed, and how children are made.
Generational replacement means the whole population is replaced.
Elitism copies the best across, unchanged.
In steady-state, one child replaces the weakest.
A child with fitness zero point five arrives. Who gets replaced?
The first-weaker method stops early. The weakest method checks all five.
The zero point one survives, so more variety is kept.
Each row is a generation. Orange shows copies of the best.
Only selection acts here: no mutation, and no crossover.
Too weak, and there is no progress. Too strong, and one copy wins.
Roulette selection: each slice is sized by fitness.
The bigger the slice, the likelier the pick.
One super-fit individual takes ninety-nine percent of the wheel.
So it is picked again and again.
With roulette, the super-fit individual takes ninety-nine percent.
Rank selection only counts the order, not the gaps.
The exponent b turns the pressure up, or down.
Tournament: draw two at random. The better one wins.
The best individual was not even drawn.
A bigger t means tougher competition.
The best wins more often as t grows.
Each encoding needs its own kind of mutation.
Re-rolling a tour breaks it: D appears twice, and J is lost.
Swapping two genes keeps every city exactly once.
One-point crossover: cut, and swap the tails.
Two-point crossover: swap the middle part.
Uniform crossover: a one in the mask swaps that gene.
Let's put it together, and evolve a picture. Fitness counts matching pixels, blank ones too.
Two recipes race. Both rely on mutation.
Algorithm one got there first, in this run.
Remember: the replacement strategy decides who stays.
Selection pressure must be balanced, not too weak and not too strong.
Choose mutation and crossover that fit your encoding.
